summary: An April 1 satirical proposal for a Firewall Enhancement Protocol that would let new technologies pass through firewalls without breaking their security model. It is a joke and not a real protocol.

eli5.summary: This joke proposes hiding all your Internet traffic inside ordinary web traffic, which the guard always lets through, so the guard is bypassed.

subtitle: An April 1st satire on bypassing firewalls by tunneling TCP/IP traffic inside HTTP.

tldr.problem: Firewalls block most traffic to enforce security, preventing employees from running innovative applications without IT manager approval.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3093 proposes FEP (Firewall Enhancement Protocol), which encodes entire TCP and IP packets as HTTP requests and responses. Since HTTP traffic typically passes through firewalls, any TCP/IP application can run inside HTTP, bypassing firewall restrictions while requiring cooperation from a host inside the firewall.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st joke RFC. It demonstrates how firewalls can be subverted while remaining technically "secure" (they still block external attacks). The RFC includes elaborate, humorous specifications for encoding TCP and IP header fields as ASCII HTTP headers.

facts.label: Encoding
facts.value: ASCII strings for headers, MIME for body

facts.label: Supported IP versions
facts.value: IPv4, IPv6 (IPv5 and IPv8 as jokes)

today: RFC 3093 is an April 1st informational RFC published 1 April 2001. It was a satire of firewall security policies, though HTTP tunneling has become a real technique (albeit not with this absurd specification).

sections.title: The Problem and the Joke
sections.content:
RFC 3093 is an April 1st satire on innovation versus security. The RFC notes that firewalls, designed to prevent unauthorized external access, have become barriers to innovation. If an employee like Scott and Mark want to experiment with a new application, the firewall may prevent them. The RFC proposes FEP to restore the end-to-end Internet model while maintaining the firewall's security model.

The satire is that FEP does preserve the firewall's actual security model: it still protects against external threats, because it requires cooperation from a host inside the firewall. The RFC says this with a straight face, even as it proposes bypassing every firewall rule by hiding packets in HTTP.
sections.eli5: Firewalls stop new programs. This joke says: wrap your program inside web traffic, which firewalls always allow, and no one will stop you.

sections.title: FEP Protocol Design
sections.content:
FEP encodes TCP/IP packets inside HTTP messages. A TCP/IP datagram is routed to FEP software, encoded inside an HTTP GET request or response body, and sent through the firewall on the normal HTTP port 80. At the destination, FEP software decodes the packet and reinserts it into the protocol stack.

The RFC defines elaborate ASCII encodings for TCP header fields as HTTP headers: TCP_Sport (source port as decimal), TCP_SeqNum (sequence number as hex, lowercase because "not urgent"), TCP_FlgBts (flags as capital or lowercase letters), TCP_Windex (window size), and many others. IPv4 and IPv6 headers are similarly encoded with humorous field names like IP6_Go_with_the_Flow for the unused Flow Label field.
sections.eli5: Each packet's headers are translated into fake HTTP headers with silly names, then sent as a normal web message.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The RFC claims FEP does not violate the firewall's security model because firewalls are designed to thwart external attacks, not internal threats. Since FEP requires cooperation from a host inside the firewall, external attackers cannot use it to breach the perimeter.

However, the RFC's humor is sharp: it acknowledges that FEP allows IT managers to be bypassed entirely, that users can decide what applications to run instead of administrators, and that it makes logging and debugging easier by using human-readable ASCII headers. The RFC even notes that tcpdump may become obsolete because FEP packets can be read directly.
sections.eli5: The joke is that security is only about keeping attackers out, not about IT managers controlling employees. So hiding traffic inside HTTP doesn't break security, it just breaks policies.
